replacements.24: The study compares ten process structures for budburst (BBCH07), flowering (BBCH65), veraison (BBCH81) and maturity/harvest (BBCH89). Every structure is evaluated with RAW and DEM-corrected temperature, with and without residual learning, giving 40 configurations per stage (Fig. 1). Matched phenology, weather and terrain data support group-preserving calibration and testing within five temperature-defined environmental zones. A newly designed residual model combines process states, recent weather, day length and terrain information using the existing TabM regression architecture. Paired comparisons quantify structural differences and the separate and combined gains from temperature correction and residual learning.
replacements.26: Fig. 1. Fully crossed workflow for regional grapevine phenology prediction. Matched phenology, weather and terrain data support evaluation of ten process structures under RAW or DEM-corrected temperature, each with or without residual learning. Group-preserving calibration and testing within five temperature-defined environmental zones support structural comparisons and paired correction benefits. Raw stage attainment remains separate from the 4 November scoring rule for late or unattained BBCH81/89 predictions. DEM, digital elevation model; ML, machine learning; MAE, mean absolute error.
replacements.28: Eligible monitoring records span eleven European countries, from 38.10 to 59.15°N and 4.20°W to 22.43°E, covering Atlantic, continental and Mediterranean thermal settings (Fig. 2). Lowlands, river valleys and hills provide local temperature contrasts relevant to phenology (de Rességuier et al., 2026). This observation domain is not a representative sample of European vineyard area.
replacements.33: Phenology observations came from TEMPO (Maury et al., 2023), the Deutscher Wetterdienst (DWD; Kaspar et al., 2014) and PEP725 (Templ et al., 2018; accessed 1 July 2026). PEP725 project members provided its data. Records retain source-qualified site, reported variety, country, WGS84 coordinates, calendar date and directly recorded BBCH code, with source identities and licences preserved. Inferred stages and observations before 1951 are excluded; BBCH07 and BBCH09 remain distinct (Lorenz et al., 1995).
replacements.34: Exact seven-field duplicates are removed, while different accepted dates or variety labels remain separate. Missing varieties and DWD maturity classes do not establish cultivar or plant identity. Sites sharing locations are grouped conservatively for validation.
replacements.35: Source-quality checks and reconciliation of DWD annual and immediate reports precede calendar and interval screening. Higher-control reports take precedence only for matching object and phase identifiers; equally controlled alternatives and records without quality metadata retain their ambiguity (Supplementary Methods S6).
replacements.36: The four target stages are screened against inclusive calendar windows and six interval bounds (Tables 2 and 3). Within each source-qualified site, exact variety label and year, each record requires a compatible date at every other observed target stage. Unsupported records are removed simultaneously until the checks stabilize; missing and non-target stages impose no constraint. Dates and codes are neither repaired nor inferred. These project screening bounds do not constrain model predictions (Supplementary Methods S6).
replacements.37: The revised inventory contains 75,738 retained and 1,575 quarantined target observations. Matching to unchanged weather eligibility and site assignments yields 74,618 observations at 3,169 sites and 26,443 site–years during 1951–2025 (Table 1). No surviving site changes partition. Screening was revised after preliminary model outputs became available, although its numerical rules do not use residuals. Historical comparisons therefore combine changes in eligibility and calibration procedures (Supplementary Sections S5–S6; Table S4).
replacements.38: Complete developmental sequences and minimum record lengths are not required. BBCH89 is a source-dependent maturity/harvest endpoint that may reflect management. Country–stage counts appear in Supplementary Table S1. Figure 2 depicts the earlier phenology-only inventory; Fig. 4 depicts the active modelling population and its unchanged environmental-zone assignments.
replacements.43: Daily mean 2-m ERA5-Land temperature at its native 0.1° grid supplies forcing in degrees Celsius (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021; Copernicus Climate Change Service, 2019a). Point assignments follow the native sampling transform. Missing dates are neither interpolated nor replaced by nearby-site values (Supplementary Section S2).
replacements.44: Every retained site–year has finite daily temperatures from 4 June of the preceding year through 31 December of the observation year, covering chilling and 90-day residual-model weather histories. Incomplete seasons are excluded. All model configurations share the retained observations; matching and temperature-consistency checks are detailed in Supplementary Section S2.
replacements.46: Copernicus GLO-30 supplies elevation from the containing native pixel, slope and aspect from a 3×3-pixel neighbourhood, and local elevation variability as the population standard deviation within an 11×11 neighbourhood (European Space Agency and Airbus, 2022). Northness and eastness encode aspect. Incomplete neighbourhoods retain missing derivatives or reduced pixel support; missing predictors are handled within residual-training folds. ERA5-Land grid elevation is invariant geopotential divided by 9.80665 m s⁻², distinct from mean GLO-30 elevation within a grid cell (Supplementary Section S2).
replacements.48: The DEM correction adjusts RAW daily temperature for the site–grid elevation difference using a fixed lapse rate of 0.0065 °C m⁻¹. This conventional gradient is not estimated locally (Rolland, 2003):
replacements.50: where T_DEM,d and T_RAW,d are corrected and raw daily mean temperatures (°C), and z_site and z_grid are GLO-30 site and ERA5-Land grid elevations (m), respectively (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021; European Space Agency and Airbus, 2022). Local inversions and seasonal lapse-rate variation are not represented. Forcing and chilling requirements are recalibrated separately under each temperature input on identical observations; response parameters remain fixed. The contrast measures prediction after recalibration and does not independently establish local temperature accuracy.
replacements.53: The ten structures combine linear or beta forcing alone (FL, FB) with four chilling–forcing combinations under sequential (-S) or parallel (-P) interaction (Table 4). All ten enter both temperature and residual-learning comparisons. Shared temperature-response components remain fixed, while accumulation requirements are calibrated by structure and temperature input.
replacements.54: Linear forcing accumulates max(T−0,0) degree-days. Its 0 °C base follows GFV, with extension beyond flowering and veraison treated as an adaptation (Parker et al., 2011). Normalized beta forcing is zero outside 0–35 °C and peaks at one at 25.4 °C (Fila et al., 2014). Triangular (CL) and beta (CB) chilling share cardinals of −1.7, 1.7 and 13.2 °C and responses bounded by zero and one. The triangular shape follows de Wergifosse et al. (2020), with cardinals transferred from Fila et al. (2014). These fixed functions control the structural comparison; they are not universal physiological constants (Fig. 3; Supplementary Methods S7).
replacements.57: In Eq. 2, Ds is the predicted date of stage s, τs its accumulation start, ws,u the competence weight, Rf,s(Tu) the forcing response to daily temperature Tu, and Hs the calibrated requirement; t is the first day when the sum over days u reaches Hs. Forcing-only models start on 1 January. Accumulation resets after each predicted stage and resumes the next day, discarding overshoot; observed dates never initialize later stages. Simulation ends on 31 December, leaving unattained and subsequent stages unpredicted (Supplementary Methods S7).
replacements.60: In Eq. 3, Kt is forcing competence on day t, C(t−1) is chilling accumulated through the preceding day and Ccrit is the fitted chilling requirement. The formulation adapts Liu et al. (2018), with minimum competence fixed at 0.2. Parallel budburst can precede full chilling competence. Later-stage weights equal one in every structure (Supplementary Methods S7).
replacements.61: Stage-specific forcing requirements and the additional chilling requirement are shared across sites, years and reported varieties. Numerical bounds are 0.001–3000 °C d for linear forcing and 0.001–200 daily response units for beta forcing and chilling. Response cardinals, calendar origins and minimum parallel competence remain fixed (Supplementary Table S3; Methods S7).
replacements.64: In Eq. 4, θ is the vector of calibrated requirements; As and Bs are equal-site MAE and signed bias for stage s. The objective averages As across BBCH07, BBCH65 and BBCH81, subject to at least 99% raw attainment both across records and in the mean of site attainment fractions for each stage. A first search minimizes the largest absolute-bias excess above one day. If feasible, a second search minimizes Eq. 4 while preserving bias and attainment constraints; otherwise, the best coverage-admissible candidate retains its recorded unmet bias target. BBCH89 enters neither the objective nor these constraints.
replacements.65: Scoring uses 4 November of each observation year, the latest calibration BBCH89 month–day, frozen across cross-fitting folds. Late or unattained raw BBCH81/89 predictions receive this administrative scoring date; BBCH81 assignment also assigns BBCH89. Early fitting uses scored BBCH81 dates while its attainment constraint uses raw dates. Assignment never restarts accumulation or replaces raw predictions, and observation-screening bounds never clip predictions.
replacements.66: After early fitting, H07, H65, H81 and any chilling requirement are frozen. Eligible calibration BBCH89 observations supply positive finite forcing sums from the day after raw predicted BBCH81 to observed maturity within the weather record. Each receives reciprocal within-site eligible-record weight. The lower weighted median, clipped to numerical bounds, defines H89. Early-stage raw predictions remain unchanged; maturity has no full-attainment constraint (Supplementary Methods S7).
replacements.67: Differential evolution calibrates each structure and temperature treatment independently. Search settings, calibration-only retries, initialization and diagnostics are specified in Supplementary Methods S7; optimizer convergence, raw attainment and bias-target feasibility are recorded separately.
replacements.71: The residual model combines process-predicted timing and phase duration with recent weather, day length and terrain to estimate remaining stage-specific errors. This design uses the existing TabM architecture (Gorishniy et al., 2025) to learn observed-minus-process calendar-day residuals. The preliminary hybrid date is
replacements.73: In Eq. 5, D̃i is the preliminary hybrid date, D̂proc,i the raw process date and r̂i the predicted residual for observation i. Residuals round to integer days, with half-day ties rounded to the nearest even integer. Each attained corrected stage must follow its preceding attained corrected stage by at least one day; unattained stages remain missing. Unconstrained dates and ordering adjustments support sensitivity analysis. Observation-screening bounds never clip predictions, and the same 4 November scoring rule applies after correction and ordering.
replacements.74: Targets use raw, unassigned out-of-fold process dates. Four grouped calibration folds generate four ordinary refits excluding one fold and six nested refits excluding each unordered pair. For neural validation fold h, training observations in fold k use the process fit excluding h and k; validation observations use the fit excluding h. Thus neither the target observation nor neural-validation labels enter its residual-training process fit. Every refit repeats early calibration and median-maturity estimation with the frozen cutoff, initialized from fixed responses and predeclared small thresholds rather than excluded-fold estimates (Supplementary Methods S7–S8).
replacements.75: Imputation, standardization and numerical embeddings use neural-training data only. Four inner folds select training duration. Final learners use all ordinary out-of-fold calibration residuals and the locked full-calibration process model. Unattained stages supply no residual targets or learned corrections. Both components remain fixed during testing.
replacements.76: The twenty numerical predictors are process-predicted day index and inclusive phase duration; temperature mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum over preceding 7-, 30- and 90-day windows; day length; and elevation, slope, northness, eastness and local elevation variability. Weather windows end on predicted dates, never observed validation dates. Estimates are retrospective, conditional on realized weather, without a fixed advance forecast issue date.
replacements.77: Training minimizes site-weighted squared residual error, whereas epoch selection minimizes site-weighted MAE of the TabM ensemble mean. Final predictions average ensemble members and three seeds. Architecture, optimizer settings and epoch selection are detailed in Supplementary Methods S8; inner-fold scores support tuning rather than unbiased performance estimation.
replacements.80: The matched population contains 74,618 observations at 3,169 sites in 11 countries and 26,443 site–years (1951–2025). Calibration contains 59,472 observations at 2,534 sites in 1,434 groups; testing contains 15,146 observations at 635 sites in 357 groups. Test-stage counts are 5,073, 5,469, 3,754 and 850 for BBCH07, BBCH65, BBCH81 and BBCH89, respectively (Supplementary Table S2). All configurations share these partitions.
replacements.81: Germany contributes 74.7% of observations and France 18.6%; France supplies 93.7% of maturity/harvest observations and Germany none. Testing covers seven countries and 21 country–stage combinations, eleven with fewer than ten eligible groups. This imbalance limits regional precision and stage comparisons (Supplementary Section S10; Tables S1, S2 and S6).
replacements.83: Approximately 80% of sites are assigned to calibration and 20% to testing within five environmental zones. Zones derive from k-means clustering of standardized monthly RAW temperature profiles for 1991–2020 (Copernicus Climate Change Service, 2019b), with each of 1,792 unique ERA5-Land cells represented once. Labels follow annual mean centroid temperature. Climate covariates alone define zones before partitioning, without phenology dates, country labels or errors (Supplementary Section S3).
replacements.84: Transitive groups connect sites sharing a weather cell, exact coordinates or coordinates rounded to four decimal places. Multi-cell groups use their mean standardized unique-cell profile for zone assignment. Within-zone allocation preserves whole groups and collective four-stage support; revised screening leaves surviving assignments unchanged. Four group-preserving, zone-balanced calibration folds contain every stage and govern ordinary and nested cross-fitting. Figure 4 shows the zones and primary allocation; detailed allocation settings appear in Supplementary Section S3.
replacements.85: The primary split evaluates held-out sites within sampled climatic conditions. Calibration, residual training and epoch selection exclude test labels. Country and zone summaries describe subsets of this holdout, not independent regional-transfer tests. Historical spatial-block, warm-year, warm-site and unstratified protocols do not evaluate the final median-cutoff and residual-learning models.
replacements.89: For each process structure and residual-learning option, MAE_RAW−MAE_DEM measures elevation-correction benefit on paired held-out observations; positive values indicate improvement. Each temperature arm is calibrated separately on identical observations. Comparing this benefit between process-only and hybrid models assesses their combined predictive contribution.
replacements.90: Terrain strata use local elevation standard deviation and absolute site–grid elevation mismatch. One-third and two-thirds quantiles across calibration sites, each represented once, define common cutpoints. With linearly interpolated quantiles, low values satisfy x≤q1/3, middle values q1/3<x≤q2/3, and high values x>q2/3. Missing values form a separate category; tied cutpoints remain unchanged. Test data and errors never determine boundaries.
replacements.91: The process DEM comparison requires common finite scoring errors across all ten structures and both inputs. Losses are averaged across fixed structures, within sites, equally across sites and equally across four stages. Additional exploratory contrasts use signed elevation mismatch, elevation, slope, northness and eastness. Supported regional semivariogram sills describe terrain at 20-km support, separately from local variability (Supplementary Methods S13). These comparisons evaluate elevation correction at fixed weather resolution (Zhao et al., 2015).
replacements.92: High-minus-low terrain contrasts use identical group-bootstrap draws and require ten contributing groups per stage in each stratum. Sensitivities exclude the coldest zone or any observation assigned a cutoff in a process temperature arm, or give groups equal weight after within-site and within-group averaging. They change scoring populations or weights without refitting. Terrain associations describe predictive differences, not causal effects or independent temperature accuracy.
replacements.94: All calibrated parameters remain fixed during testing. Paired factorial comparisons distinguish RAW and DEM process-only predictions from RAW and DEM hybrids across all ten structures. Test observations support performance assessment and subsequent rankings.
replacements.95: Individual process-model summaries use each configuration’s finite scoring dates, with raw attainment and missingness reported separately. Paired factorial summaries instead require common finite populations.
replacements.96: Structural comparisons use RAW process predictions in 21 fixed pairs: linear versus beta forcing (five), triangular versus beta chilling (four), sequential versus parallel interaction (four), and absent versus present chilling (eight). Each family requires finite scoring errors for every constituent model. Losses are averaged across equal-weight pairs, within sites and equally across sites and stages. Right-minus-left MAE changes describe aggregate component contrasts; models are neither independent replicates nor an ensemble prediction (Supplementary Section S9; Table S5).
replacements.97: RAW residual-learning contrasts compare RAW process and hybrid predictions; hybrid DEM contrasts compare separately fitted RAW and DEM hybrids. Both arms must have finite scoring errors in all ten structures. These contrasts and the process DEM contrast share 15,105 observations at 633 sites in 355 groups, enabling paired comparison of DEM benefits. Individual-model contrasts retain the same mask; aggregate losses average across the ten fixed structures before site and stage averaging (Supplementary Section S15).
replacements.100: In Eq. 6, P and H denote process-only and hybrid predictions, and RAW and DEM denote temperature inputs. Positive ΔG indicates a smaller DEM benefit after residual learning. The same group multiplicities enter both benefits in each bootstrap draw; intervals derive from their paired difference. Percentage gains use each workflow’s own RAW MAE. Baseline–gain associations are descriptive because gains contain baseline error arithmetically.
replacements.101: Spatial summaries describe CB-FL-S, the lowest-MAE RAW process model in the primary test comparison. Site-error medians and interquartile ranges describe distributions; zone means weight sites equally within stage. Sparse zones retain descriptive estimates and support counts, while missing stages preclude overall averages. This analysis supplies no independent validation of model selection or zone-specific calibration (Supplementary Section S9).
replacements.104: In Eq. 7, sums extend over observations i and sites j within stage s; ei,j,s is predicted-minus-observed calendar-day error and wi,j,s gives equal total weight to each site. Positive bias indicates late predictions and negative bias early predictions. MAE measures error magnitude; bias can conceal opposing errors. Overall MAE and bias average all four stage estimates equally.
replacements.105: Calendar-date differences preserve cross-year offsets and leap days. Record, site and group counts accompany comparisons. Raw-date summaries use attained predictions; scoring summaries apply the 4 November rule to BBCH81/89, with assignment, raw attainment and attainment by cutoff reported separately. Full-calibration summaries describe apparent training performance, not out-of-fold accuracy.
replacements.106: Paired intervals use 2,000 bootstrap draws of original independence groups (seed 20260913), retaining all member sites and multiplying equal-site weights by group draw frequency. Stage intervals require at least ten contributing groups; overall intervals require this support in every stage. Pointwise 95% percentile intervals require at least 95% finite draws and have no multiplicity adjustment. Smaller samples retain descriptive estimates. Calibration intervals concern apparent fitted-model differences; test intervals concern the primary held-out population.

Original main P83–84 supply these details. S3 presently covers the general grouping/clustering principles and active counts, but not these settings.
